title: LangVersion, TFM, and breaking changes
hook: Module 01 told you not to set `LangVersion` to `latest`. This page is why CI boxes lie, and what “breaking change” means when only the compiler moved.

sections.heading: TFM picks the language; csproj can override
sections.prose: SDK projects pair a target framework with a default language: `net8.0` → C# 12, `net9.0` → C# 13, `net10.0` → C# 14. Visual Studio disables the language dropdown for that reason. A newer LangVersion than the TFM is unsupported — you may parse syntax whose runtime APIs do not exist. Override in the csproj or `Directory.Build.props` with `preview` or `14.0` when you mean it. `latest` means whatever compiler is installed on that agent; two GitHub runners can accept different syntax. `latestMajor`/`default` track the compiler’s latest major, still not a pinned TFM. `#error version` (case sensitive) prints compiler and language versions as CS8304. File-based apps (module 01) inherit the SDK’s defaults unless `#:property` says otherwise.

snippets.label: Pin net10.0, do not pin latest
snippets.code:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <!-- <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>  -->
    <!-- <LangVersion>14.0</LangVersion> only if you must document it -->
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
snippets.explanation: net10.0 already means C# 14 on a current SDK. Explicit latest is how a laptop with a preview SDK ships syntax CI cannot build.

sections.heading: Compiler breaking changes are not BCL breaking changes
sections.prose: Raising C# can change overload resolution, definite assignment, and how identifiers bind. C# 14’s `field` token inside accessors shadows a member named `field` — Microsoft documents `@field` / `this.field` as the escape. Null-conditional assignment changes evaluation of the right-hand side. Method-group natural type tightened in C# 13. These are listed in the compiler breaking-changes notes (Roslyn / “Breaking changes in the C# compiler”), separate from .NET runtime breaking changes. A library compiled with C# 14 can still target an older TFM only if you stay in the supported pairing; do not assume binaries are a free pass to newer syntax on older runtimes.

snippets.label: field keyword collision
snippets.explanation: Rename the member. Do not ship a property named around the collision. Call this out in a LangVersion bump PR.

sections.heading: What CI should lock
sections.prose: Lock the SDK with `global.json`. Lock the TFM in the csproj. Treat PublicAPI files (module 16) as a third lock for libraries. Analyzers that fire on new language rules should be upgraded deliberately; an SDK bump that silently enables a warning-as-error is a breaking change for the repo even if the language spec calls it a bug fix. Read the C# 14 breaking-changes article before you merge `net10.0`.

interviewTakeaways: Language version follows TFM; net10.0 is C# 14. Avoid LangVersion=latest.
Compiler breaking changes (field, overload resolution) are documented separately from runtime breaks.
global.json plus TFM plus public API baselines make the bump reviewable.
commonPitfalls: Directory.Build.props LangVersion shared with VB projects — the numbers are not the same language.
Raising LangVersion to use span conversions while staying on net8.0 and then hitting missing runtime support.
Ignoring #error version when two agents disagree.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `typescript` package vs `lib` vs `@types/node` is the same three-lock problem as SDK vs LangVersion vs TFM. `latest` in either ecosystem is a reproducibility smell.
